prompt: Which part of ITIL 4's definition of a service does the lesson call the important one?

choices.text: Not having to manage costs and risks
choices.why: Right. The clinic wants bookings, not servers and backups.

choices.text: A means of enabling value co-creation
choices.why: That opens the definition; the lesson stresses the end.
Uptime is not in the definition.
The definition does not name who delivers.

prompt: Which of these are among ITIL 4's seven guiding principles? Choose all that apply.
hint: Several would fit the agile manifesto.

choices.why: Yes.
Yes.
Yes.

choices.text: Approve every change at a weekly board
choices.why: Not a principle, and ITIL 4 no longer prescribes a board.

choices.text: Document every service before it runs
choices.why: Not one of the seven.

prompt: What did ITIL 4 replace the version 3 service lifecycle with?

choices.why: The lifecycle was the thing replaced.
That is PMBOK's sixth edition.
Right. Principles, a value chain, practices and continual improvement.
ITIL borrowed ideas from agile; it did not adopt Scrum.

prompt: Booking has stopped in one clinic. What is the goal of incident management right now?

choices.text: Find the root cause before touching anything
choices.why: That keeps users waiting while logs are read.

choices.text: Restore normal service as quickly as possible
choices.why: Right. Finding the cause is problem management's job.
The SLA is not what an incident changes.
A change may come later; restoring comes first.

prompt: Match each ITIL term to its meaning.

pairs.right: An unplanned interruption or loss of quality
A cause, or potential cause, of incidents
A problem analysed but not yet fixed
Steps that restore service until the fix

prompt: Reminders fail every Monday and the help desk restarts the job each time. What is missing, by the lesson?

choices.text: A service level agreement signed with every clinic
choices.why: An SLA would not find the cause.
Incidents are being handled; the restart restores service.
A faster workaround still leaves the fault.
Right. Each incident is resolved; nobody is investigating the cause.

prompt: Why does the lesson call the problem records the most honest document about a system?
hint: Who writes them, and about what?

choices.text: They are audited by an external body
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.
Right. They list design decisions that did not hold up in production, written by the people who pay for them.

choices.text: They are written by the architect
choices.why: They are written by the people who operate the system.

choices.text: They contain no opinions, only numbers
choices.why: They contain analysis and workarounds.

prompt: An incident has high impact and low urgency. What priority does the lesson's matrix give it?
What priority does the matrix give medium impact and low urgency?
hint: One step down on impact, two on urgency.

prompt: A director's report fails; it affects one person and is due next week. What does the matrix protect the help desk from?

choices.why: Right. It gets the priority the table gives it, like anybody else's.
Unrelated to ranking incidents.
Every incident is recorded.
The SLA sets targets per priority; it protects nobody from pressure.

prompt: Every incident in a team's queue is priority 1. What does the lesson say is missing?

choices.why: Change approval is unrelated to incident priority.

choices.text: More people on the help desk
choices.why: Staffing does not fix a matrix that sorts nothing.
More levels inflate the same way.

choices.text: Agreed definitions of impact and urgency
choices.why: Right. Without them, everybody marks high to get attention, and nothing is sorted.

prompt: Match each type of change to its route.

pairs.right: Assessed and authorised by a change authority

prompt: Why was the practice renamed change enablement?

choices.text: Because ITIL 4 dropped change control entirely
choices.why: The practice still controls change.
Right. Its purpose is to let changes happen safely, not to stop them.

choices.text: Because changes now need two approvals
choices.why: Nothing about the number of approvals.
Scrum has no such term.

prompt: A deployment has been done fifty times with the same automated procedure and no failures, and still waits for a weekly board. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Treat it as an emergency change to go faster
choices.why: Emergencies are for urgent fixes, not a shortcut.
Standard changes are still recorded.
Right. The weekly wait adds lead time and no safety.

choices.text: Keep it normal, since every change is risky
choices.why: Its record shows this class is not.

prompt: A physiotherapist forgot their password. How should ITIL record it?

choices.why: There is no cause to investigate.
Right. Logged as incidents, requests would distort the failure statistics.
Nothing in the service changes.
It is not an interruption of the service.

prompt: An SLA promises 99.5% availability; the hosting contract guarantees 99%. What is wrong?

choices.why: Right. Check underpinning contracts before signing an SLA.

choices.text: Nothing; the SLA is with the customer
choices.why: The customer's target depends on the supplier's.

choices.text: 99.5% is too low for any SLA
choices.why: The figure is fine; the mismatch is the issue.

choices.text: The OLA should be signed with the hosting company
choices.why: An OLA is internal; the hosting one is a contract.

prompt: What is the watermelon effect?

choices.why: An unsigned SLA is a different problem.
That distorts statistics, but it is not this effect.

choices.text: Targets that change colour each month
choices.why: It is about what the targets miss.
Right. The targets measure what was easy, not what users feel.

prompt: Booking runs 14 hours a day over a 30-day month. How many minutes of unavailability does 99.5% availability allow in the month?
What did the research summarised in Accelerate find about approval of changes by an external body?
hint: Delivery got worse; failures did not fall.

choices.why: Delivery was worse.

choices.text: Fewer failed changes, at the cost of speed
choices.why: It found no link to the failure rate.

choices.text: Worse delivery, and no fewer failed changes
choices.why: Right. Lightweight review close to the work plus automated tests was recommended instead.
There was an effect on delivery.

prompt: How does the lesson describe an automated pipeline with tests, peer review and rollback, in ITIL's terms?

choices.text: An emergency change, because it is fast
choices.why: Speed does not make a change an emergency.
Incidents still happen and must be handled.
Right. Approved once, executed every time.
ITIL 4 asks to optimise and automate.

prompt: Which design questions does the lesson tie to incident management? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Which programming language is it written in?
choices.why: Not one of the lesson's questions.

choices.text: Can it be restored without a fix?
choices.why: Yes: designed-in workarounds.

choices.text: Can the system tell you it is broken?
choices.why: Yes: detection.
Yes: containment.

prompt: A failure in SMS reminders also stops bookings. What does the lesson say the design has done?

choices.text: Nothing unusual; features depend on each other
choices.why: The coupling is the defect.
It created a bigger incident, not a change.

choices.text: Met the SLA, since booking is restored when SMS returns
choices.why: Booking was down; the SLA is breached meanwhile.

choices.text: Turned a priority 4 into a priority 1
choices.why: Right. A design that cannot fail in parts raises the impact of every failure.

prompt: Order a user's encounter with ITIL's practices as the lesson presents them.
trap: The cause is found before the fix is deployed; restoring comes first of all.

prompt: A problem whose cause is known but not yet fixed is a known ___.
